mainEntity.name: How do I know if my dental crown is cracked?

acceptedAnswer.text: A cracked crown may not always be obvious, particularly in the early stages. Signs that may indicate a problem include a change in how your bite feels, sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweet foods, a rough or sharp texture when you run your tongue across the tooth, or a visible line or chip on the crown surface. In many cases, a crack is identified only during a routine dental examination or on a dental X-ray. If you notice any of these signs, booking a dental review is a sensible step, even if you are not experiencing pain.

mainEntity.name: Can a cracked crown lead to further problems if left unassessed?

acceptedAnswer.text: If a crown develops a crack or the seal at the crown margin becomes compromised, it can create a pathway for bacteria to enter beneath the restoration. Over time, this may lead to secondary decay affecting the underlying tooth, sensitivity, or in some cases, infection within the tooth root. Identifying and addressing a cracked crown early is generally preferable, as it reduces the risk of these complications developing. Your dentist can assess the extent of any damage and advise on appropriate management following a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: Will a cracked crown always need to be replaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily — the appropriate management of a cracked crown depends on a number of factors, including the location and severity of the crack, the condition of the underlying tooth, and whether the crown margin has been affected. In some cases, minor damage may be monitored or addressed conservatively. In other circumstances, replacement of the crown may be recommended to restore full protection and function. Treatment suitability is always determined following a clinical assessment, and your dentist will discuss the available options with you based on your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible for a crown to crack on its own without any trauma?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a crown can develop cracks without any single dramatic event or obvious injury. Gradual wear from everyday biting and chewing, repeated low-level forces from tooth grinding, changes in bite alignment over time, or simply the natural ageing of the material can all contribute to crown damage without any specific incident. This is one reason why regular dental examinations are important — they allow your dentist to monitor restorations over time and identify changes that may not produce noticeable symptoms in the early stages.

mainEntity.name: Does the material of a crown affect how likely it is to crack?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, different crown materials have different properties in terms of strength, flexibility, and resistance to fracture. Porcelain and all-ceramic crowns offer excellent aesthetics and are well-suited to many situations, but they can be more susceptible to cracking under heavy biting forces compared to metal or porcelain-fused-to-metal restorations. Your dentist will consider your individual circumstances — including your bite, whether you grind your teeth, and the position of the tooth in your mouth — when advising on the most suitable crown material for your needs.

mainEntity.name: Can I still attend my regular dentist appointment if I suspect a cracked crown but have no pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — in fact, a routine dental appointment is exactly the right place to raise any concerns about your crown, even in the absence of pain. Your dentist can examine the crown visually, assess the margins, check your bite, and take X-rays if appropriate to gain a clearer picture of the crown's condition. You can also mention any changes in sensation or bite that you have noticed, however minor they may seem. Early identification of any issues allows for timely and often more straightforward management. If you are currently due a check-up, this is a good opportunity to book an appointment with a dentist in London and have any questions addressed in person.
